newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Political concerns drag on Europe most.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Political concerns drag on Europe most.

text.p: Politics will weigh heavily on European bond markets, while on the other side of the Atlantic nagging worries about fundamentals will be the over-riding factor, analysts said on Wednesday.

Political developments have been fast and furious in Germany and France, as well as Canada, and analysts said the risk/reward ratio was poor for Europe. For Canada, which like France just had an election, the main concern was the U.S. economic outlook.
So far, European debt has been propped up by domestic investors' appetite for fixed income assets.

This is despite a left wing election victory in France, which analysts said threatened to disrupt the single European currency process. And in Germany, the government has been engaged in a damaging battle with the Bundesbank over gold valuations and budget measures.
"It's like a David and Goliath fight, hedge funds versus domestic liquidity," said Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London.
"We've got all the right ingredients -- technicals, politics, uncertainty, you name it -- that are negative for the market, but there is no actual selling occurring," said Shah,
But he still reckoned a negative correction could come for European debt.
Shah said people had been puzzled why there had not been a bigger selloff on the back of the French election.
But the bulk of French bond investors are domestic and for now they simply are not selling. Shah said domestic demand was also helping Italy and Spain.
Stephen Lewis, London Bond Broking chief economist, said political risks in France would spill over to affect the whole of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"All of those countries which have built in a lot of hope regarding EMU will suffer from what the communists in France get up to," he said. "It is difficult to judge now whether we will end up with a weak euro or no euro at all."
Lewis said with a weak euro there would probably some benefit in the peripheral markets, whereas with no euro, Bunds would be most likely to gain in Europe.
A bond strategist at a U.S. bank in London agreed politics would continue to hold sway in continental Europe.

"We have got to see what the French cabinet is and what is going to be the real French position on EMU. We have got to see what their real intentions on this are and what the German reaction will be," he said.
He also pointed to political risks in Italy where the 1998 Italian budget will have to be decided.

"Not only has (the government) got to find savings, but it has to find them in a manner which is acceptable to its European partners, and we have to see how that plays out in the Italian political arena," he said.
The U.S. bank strategist advised looking at the short end and said there were still some opportunities for European convergence trade.
"The best example of that, Italy/Germany, has the potential to be a good trade but we need to see just a few more of these EMU questions...resolved," he said.
At 1140 GMT, the BTP/Bund yield spread was at 132 basis points, having narrowed from 172 at the beginning of the year.
But Lewis advised getting out of European bonds and looking to U.S. Treasuries.

"The risk/reward ratio in analysing European markets now is weighted much more towards the risks than towards any rewards investors are likely to make. It is probably easier to analyse situations elsewhere," he said.
"If we get inflation pressures rising, the Fed will step in and tighten policy so there is for the long term an assurance that inflation is not going to go much above its present level."
Lewis said at current levels 10-year T-note yields of over 6.5 percent were attractive.
In Canada, the ruling Liberal Party won a slim majority in parliament. Markets were generally relieved the Liberals were returned, leaving the issue of separatist politics in the background for now.
Analysts said the U.S. market's fortunes would probably dicate Canadian debt from here on in.
